Description.Summary: Glean Agents is an enterprise AI agent platform that automates workplace tasks by building, deploying, orchestrating, and governing AI agents across workflows. It functions as a horizontal environment for creating autonomous agents that handle multi-step workflows using natural language, enterprise context, and a library of actions. The platform is deployed as an enterprise SaaS product integrated into web applications, Slack, Microsoft Teams, and developer tools, supporting agents for engineering, sales, HR, and other business functions.

Glean Agents is the horizontal environment for building, deploying, orchestrating, and governing AI agents in the enterprise.

Practices.Summary: Glean evaluates agents with an evalset, a representative set of user instructions paired with ideal responses, curated with subject matter experts as a small set of about 20 real-world examples. A single north star metric is broken into simple sub-metrics graded with binary (0 or 1) scoring; for its sales prospecting agent these were completeness, personalization, tone, and groundedness.

evidence.quote: A good evaluation starts with an evalset: a representative set of user instructions paired with the ideal responses.
Start by asking a few user subject matter experts to help curate a small, high-quality set of about 20 real-world examples.
Start with a single north star metric, the most important measure of the agent’s quality or usefulness that everyone can align on.

Break your north star metric into 2–4 simple sub-metrics to grade consistently and get a clear picture of what to improve. For our sales prospecting agent, our north star was message quality, which we broke down into four components:
Completeness: Does the message have all the key ingredients?
Personalization: Is the message tailored to the prospect?
Tone: Does the message feel personal, insightful, and easy to understand?
Groundedness: Are the claims based on accurate enterprise and public data?
When it comes to grading metrics, simple binary scoring (0 or 1) works best.

Practices.Summary: Glean uses real-world user feedback such as upvotes and downvotes to validate agent performance and samples real user queries into the evalset to keep it fresh and aligned with evolving user needs.

Practices.Summary: After running an evaluation, Glean reviews the metrics and examples to spot patterns where the agent underperformed, then makes targeted changes in a set order: refine instructions, structure context (point to specific data sources, use sub-agents), tune LLM parameters such as temperature, and finally choose a different LLM.

evidence.quote: Once you’ve run your evaluation, now it’s time for the most important part: using the results to make your agent better.
Start by looking at the metrics to see where the agent underperformed, review examples to spot patterns, and then make targeted improvements.
As a rule of thumb, make agent changes in this order:
Refine instructions: The highest-impact changes often come from refining instructions.

Structure context: Control the information the agent sees by pointing it to specific data sources when general context is too broad. You can also avoid information overload by using sub-agents with their own memory.
Tune parameters: Adjust LLM parameters like temperature, which controls the agent’s creativity.
Choose LLMs: Some models really excel at certain task domains and lag in others. Swapping the LLM for a different one may provide a significant boost.

Practices.Summary: Glean advises not shying away from complex evalsets, because users push agents with multi-step tasks across multiple sources; these are not edge cases but often the most valuable jobs to be done, and testing should start with instructions the builder is unsure about.

Others.Summary: Glean favors an open, interoperable agent architecture over a single monolith: the stack is made of layers (context, models, orchestration, interfaces, and security) that can each evolve independently while working together.

evidence.quote: An open architecture mindset is different. It acknowledges that there is no single monolith that can keep pace with the speed of AI innovation.

Open, interoperable agent architectures are essential for enterprises to avoid vendor lock-in, enable rapid adoption of new AI capabilities, and ensure that each layer of the stack—context, models, orchestration, interfaces, and security—can evolve independently while working together.

Practices.Summary: Glean tracks documentation freshness with metadata update practices. Content typically appears in search within a few minutes of indexing. Crawl Rate and Change Rate metrics update approximately every 5–10 minutes, with Change Rate indicating ongoing freshness based on user-driven changes synced in the past 24 hours. The platform allows attaching structured metadata to documents from any datasource and offers a Custom Metadata API for tagging and classifying documents without re-indexing.

evidence.quote: Content typically appears in search within a few minutes of indexing.

Crawl Rate and Change Rate metrics update approximately every 5–10 minutes. Change Rate is the number of user‑driven changes synced in the past 24 hours after the initial crawl completes and indicates ongoing freshness.

Glean allows attaching structured metadata to documents from any datasource ... The platform offers a Custom Metadata API that enables tagging and classifying documents already indexed in Glean without re-indexing the source document.
